topics.title: Kathiyawadi Food and Pickles: The Role of Athanu on the Plate
topics.excerpt: Kathiyawadi food is bold, rustic and spice-forward. How athanu fits on the plate, which pickles to try, and how to pair them at home.
topics.quick_answer: Kathiyawadi food comes from the Saurashtra peninsula of Gujarat and is known for millet rotlas, garlic chutney, generous white butter and more chilli than sugar. Its pickles (athanu) are pungent and chunky to match: Gunda Keri, methia keri and spicy keri achar, with a sweet jar such as Gor Keri as the counterpoint.

p: Kathiyawad is the older name for the Saurashtra peninsula in western Gujarat, the land around Rajkot, Jamnagar, Junagadh, Bhavnagar, Amreli and Porbandar. Mainland Gujarati food is often described as gently sweet and sour. Kathiyawadi cooking is sharper and more rustic: garlic is used freely, red chilli is generous, and sugar is used with a lighter hand.

The region is dry for much of the year, and farming families built their meals around crops that suited it — bajra and jowar, groundnut and pulses. Food also had to keep, which is how pickles, dried chillies and papad earned their place in every Kathiyawadi kitchen.

sections.h2: Dishes you will meet on a Kathiyawadi thali
list: Bajra no rotlo — thick, hand-patted millet bread, usually served with a lump of white butter (makhan) and sometimes a piece of jaggery.
Sev tameta nu shaak — a tangy tomato curry finished with crisp sev just before serving.
Ringan no olo — smoky roasted brinjal mashed with garlic, green chilli and onion.
Lasaniya bateta — baby potatoes in a fiery red garlic masala.
Dahi tikhari — curd tempered with garlic and chilli, eaten with rotla or bhakhri.
Kadhi and khichdi — the comforting end of the meal, often with a spoon of pickle on the side.
Chaas — thin, salted buttermilk that cools the palate between spicy bites.

sections.h2: Why pickles matter so much here
p: In a Kathiyawadi home the pickle is not a garnish. It is one of several small sides — chutney, fried green chillies, raw onion, papad, a piece of gor — that turn plain rotla into a full meal. A dense millet bread with butter needs something sour and pungent beside it, and a spoon of athanu does that job instantly.

Pickles also follow the farming year. Raw mangoes, gunda berries and fresh methi seed come in early summer, and families traditionally made a year's supply in a few busy weeks. Those jars then carried the kitchen through monsoon and winter, when fresh produce was less varied.

sections.h2: The athanu you will find on a Kathiyawadi plate
list: Gunda Keri — raw mango with gunda (lasoda) berries; sticky, chewy and a true regional favourite.
Methia keri — raw mango in a fenugreek-led masala; bittersweet and pungent.
Chana Keri Methi — methia keri with whole chickpeas that soak up the oil and spice.
Katka Keri — small, crunchy mango pieces in a spicy mustard-chilli masala; the everyday jar.
Gor Keri and Chhundo — sweet mango pickles, served in small amounts to balance the heat. Mainland Gujarat leans on these more; Kathiyawadi kitchens reach for the spicy jar first.

p: Gunda is the small fruit of the Cordia tree, known as lasoda in Hindi. Inside, it is naturally sticky. In many homes the berries are slit, the seed is removed and the hollow is packed with masala, then mixed with raw mango pieces and oil. Over time the gunda turns soft and chewy and absorbs the spice completely.

Many people from Saurashtra remember Gunda Keri from childhood summers, when pitting the sticky berries was slow, shared work. With bajra rotla and butter, its chewy bite holds its own in a way small mango pieces sometimes do not.

sections.h2: Methia keri and Chana Keri Methi
p: Methia keri is built on split fenugreek seed (methi kuria) along with split mustard, chilli, turmeric and hing. Fenugreek is bitter on its own, but in pickle it turns pleasantly bittersweet and gives the masala a deep, almost nutty aroma.

Adding whole chana is a homely Kathiyawadi touch. The chickpeas soften in the oil, take on the masala and give the pickle a second texture beside the mango. A spoon of Chana Keri Methi stirred into hot khichdi, or eaten with kadhi and rice, is a simple meal many Gujarati families still love.

sections.h2: Building a Kathiyawadi plate at home
list: Start with bajra rotla or bhakhri, with white butter or ghee.
Add one strong shaak: sev tameta, ringan no olo or lasaniya bateta.
Put out lasan ni chutney and a few fried green chillies.
Choose one spicy pickle and one sweet pickle for balance.
Finish with kadhi-khichdi and a glass of chaas.
Bajra rotla with butter — Gunda Keri; the chewy gunda suits the dense bread.
Kadhi-khichdi — Chana Keri Methi; the fenugreek cuts through the mild, creamy meal.
Thepla or bhakhri — Katka Keri; small pieces are easy to eat with every bite.
Sev tameta or lasaniya bateta — a little Gor Keri or Chhundo, because the curry already brings the heat.
Dal-bhaat on a weekday — Katka Keri, the all-rounder.

sections.h2: Kathiyawadi dhabas and the pickle bowl
p: Over the years, Kathiyawadi-style restaurants and highway dhabas have opened across Gujarat and Maharashtra, and they have carried this food far beyond Saurashtra. Their thalis usually arrive with rotla, a couple of fiery shaak, chutney, chaas and a steel bowl of pickle on the table.
For many city families, that dhaba meal is their first taste of Kathiyawadi food and pickles together.

sections.h2: Serving and storing the Kathiyawadi way
p: Take out only what the meal needs into a small bowl, using a clean, completely dry spoon, and close the jar straight away. Keep it in a cool, dry cupboard away from the stove, and make sure the masala stays covered by its oil.

Do not waste the oil at the end of a jar. Kathiyawadi cooks drizzle it over rotla, mix it into plain khichdi or rub it on a bhakhri before serving. Follow the label on the jar for best-before guidance.

sections.h2: Where The Pickle Affair fits in
p: The Pickle Affair, a brand of Arham Foods, makes pickles from traditional Kathiawadi recipes in small batches, with no synthetic colours. To explore Kathiyawadi food and pickles at home, Gunda Keri and Chana Keri Methi Achar are the most characteristic jars, and Katka Keri covers the everyday meal.
Each product page lists ingredients and storage advice, so check them if you have specific preferences before you order.

faqs: What is Kathiyawadi food?
It is the cuisine of the Saurashtra peninsula in Gujarat — bold, garlic- and chilli-forward cooking built around millet rotlas, white butter, hearty shaak, kadhi-khichdi and buttermilk.
Which pickle is most typical of Kathiyawadi food?
Gunda Keri and methia keri are among the most traditional, with spicy keri achar as the everyday jar. A sweet pickle such as Gor Keri is usually served alongside in small amounts.
Is Kathiyawadi food sweet like other Gujarati food?
Less so. It leans spicier and more garlic-forward, and sugar is used more sparingly than in many mainland Gujarati dishes.
What is the difference between Kathiyawadi and Kathiawadi?
They are two English spellings of the same word. Both refer to the Kathiyawad region, also called Saurashtra.
Which pickle goes best with bajra rotla?
Gunda Keri is the classic choice because its chewy texture suits the dense bread. Methia keri also works well, especially with a little white butter.
Can I eat Kathiyawadi pickles if I do not like very spicy food?
Yes. Take a small piece at a time, eat it with rotla, rice or curd, and keep a sweet pickle such as Gor Keri or Chhundo on the side.
topics.conclusion: Kathiyawadi food and pickles belong together: a dense rotla, a fiery shaak and a spoon of pungent athanu make the meal. Start with Gunda Keri or Chana Keri Methi Achar for the real regional taste, and keep a sweet jar nearby for balance.

topics.title: Mango Pickle Season: Why Achar Is Made in April to June
topics.excerpt: Why Indian families make mango pickle in early summer, how the season shapes the jar, and what it means when you buy or store achar.
topics.quick_answer: Mango pickle season falls in early summer, roughly April to June in Gujarat and Maharashtra, because that is when raw mangoes are firm, sour and plentiful and the dry sun helps dry the salted pieces. Families finish before the monsoon brings humidity, and the pickle made then is meant to be eaten through the year.

sections.h2: Why early summer is mango pickle season
p: A pickling mango has to be raw, firm and sharply sour. That stage comes after the trees flower in late winter and the fruit has grown to full size, but before it starts to ripen and soften. In Gujarat and Maharashtra this usually lands between April and early June, though the exact weeks shift with the region, the variety and the weather each year.
Once mangoes turn sweet and yellow inside, they suit aamras better than achar, so pickle-makers buy when the fruit is hardest and most sour.

sections.h2: The sun, the heat and the race against monsoon
p: The same months bring the strongest, driest sun of the year. Traditional kitchens use it to dry salted mango pieces, to dissolve sugar or jaggery in sweet pickles, and to warm jars while the masala settles into the fruit.

Timing matters at the other end too. Once the monsoon arrives, the air turns humid, and moisture is the main enemy of pickle. Families try to finish their pickling, and have the jars sealed and stored, before the first heavy rains.

sections.h2: A pickle year at a glance
list: Late winter — mango trees flower and small fruit begins to set.
Early spring — tender young mangoes appear; some homes make quick, small-batch pickles from them.
Early summer — full-sized raw mangoes flood the market; this is the main window for keri achar, Chhundo and Gor Keri.
Monsoon — pickling stops, jars rest in a cool, dry place and the flavours mature.
Winter and beyond — the summer batch is eaten daily, often at its most rounded and balanced.

sections.h2: The seasonal rhythm in a pickle kitchen
list: Buy raw mangoes at their firmest and sourest, and process them within a day or two.
Wash the fruit and dry every piece completely; even a little water left on the skin can spoil a batch.
Cut the mango to suit the style — small cubes for katka, larger chunks for keri achar, grated for Chhundo.
Rub with salt and turmeric and rest so the pieces release their water.
Drain, then spread the pieces on clean cloth to dry in the sun or in a warm, airy room.
Mix with masala and oil, fill clean, dry jars and leave the pickle to mature.

p: Within the season, the order often follows the fruit. Spicy keri achar and katka-style pickles are made once mangoes are full-sized and very sour. Sweet pickles such as Chhundo and Gor Keri use the same raw mangoes, and in many homes the jar is set out in the sun for some days so the sugar or jaggery dissolves into a thick syrup.

Gunda Keri depends on a second crop: gunda (lasoda) berries, which have their own short season around the same time. If you miss the gunda, you wait a year, which is part of why Gunda Keri feels special.

sections.h2: Pickle season as a family tradition
p: In many Gujarati homes, pickle season is a household event. Mangoes are bought in bulk, someone sits with the large hand cutter (sudi) cutting pieces, children are sent to guard the drying cloth on the terrace, and the eldest woman of the house decides when the salt and masala taste right.
Once the jars are ready, some are shared with married daughters, neighbours and relatives in other cities.

sections.h2: When the weather does not cooperate
list: Unseasonal rain — cooks bring the pieces indoors and dry them under a fan rather than packing them damp.
Cloudy, humid days — drying takes longer; patience is better than rushing the mix.
An early monsoon — some families make smaller batches or skip a style that needs long sun.
Extreme heat — pieces are turned and checked so they dry evenly without scorching.

sections.h2: Why a summer pickle tastes good all year
p: A pickle made in mango pickle season is not meant to be eaten that week. In the first days the masala tastes raw and sharp and the mango is very crisp. Over the following weeks the salt, oil and spices move into the fruit, the mustard mellows, and the sourness becomes rounder.

Salt, oil, spices and dryness are what keep a traditional pickle, which is why a well-made summer batch can be enjoyed long after the mangoes have left the market. Some softening of the pieces over the months is a normal part of that maturing.

sections.h2: What the season means when you buy
p: Because raw mangoes are a seasonal crop, pickle-makers prepare their mango pickles around the summer harvest. You do not need a jar that was 'made this week' — a pickle that has had time to mature often tastes better.

What matters is how the jar has been made and stored. Read the label for packing and best-before details, and buy from makers who are clear about who they are and where they pack. The Pickle Affair's Homemade Mango Pickle, Katka Keri and Gor Keri follow traditional Kathiawadi recipes and are made in small batches.

sections.h2: Keeping your jar happy through the monsoon
list: Store the jar in a cool, dry cupboard, away from the stove and sink.
Use a clean, completely dry spoon every time, and never put a wet spoon back in.
Close the lid firmly straight after use; humid air is the bigger risk during monsoon.
Keep the masala covered with its oil and press pieces down if they rise above it.
Check the jar now and then; mould, fizzing or an off smell mean it should be discarded.

p: The timing is similar across much of India. In Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, summer is when families make avakaya. In the Konkan, raw mangoes go into spicy pickles before the rains. In Punjab and other parts of the north, raw mango achar is made as the summer crop arrives.
Each region uses its own mangoes, oils and spice mixes, so the jars taste very different, but the logic is the same everywhere: catch the mango raw, use the summer sun, and finish before the monsoon.

faqs: When is mango pickle made in India?
Mostly in early summer, roughly April to June in Gujarat and Maharashtra, when raw mangoes are firm and sour and the sun is strong. The exact weeks vary by region and year.
Why is mango pickle not made during the monsoon?
Humid air makes it hard to dry the mango pieces and increases the risk of spoilage, so families finish pickling before the rains.
Is pickle made in summer good all year?
Yes, if it is properly made and stored. Its flavour matures over time. Follow the label on the jar for best-before guidance.
Which mango is used for pickle in Gujarat?
Firm, sour raw varieties such as Rajapuri are traditional. Sweet table mangoes soften too quickly for pickle.
Should I buy pickle only during mango season?
No. Pickle is made in season so that it can be enjoyed through the year. Focus on a trustworthy maker and good storage at home.
Why does my mango pickle taste different later in the year?
The masala keeps moving into the fruit, so the mango softens slightly and the flavour becomes rounder and less sharp. That is normal maturing, not spoilage.
topics.conclusion: Mango pickle season is a short summer window that feeds the whole year. Choose jars from makers who follow traditional methods, store them dry and cool, and enjoy how the flavour deepens with time.

topics.title: Rajapuri Mango for Pickle: Why Gujarat Uses This Variety
topics.excerpt: Why Gujarati kitchens prefer Rajapuri and other firm, sour mangoes for achar, how to pick them at the market, and why Alphonso and Kesar fall short.
topics.quick_answer: Rajapuri is a large, firm, sour mango variety grown in Gujarat and widely preferred for pickles. When raw, its thick flesh stays crisp through salting and drying, and its sharp sourness carries the masala. Sweet table mangoes such as Alphonso and Kesar soften quickly and turn mushy in achar.

p: Rajapuri is one of the best-known mango varieties of Gujarat. The fruit is large and heavy, with thick flesh and a relatively small stone for its size. It can be eaten ripe, but its real reputation is as a raw pickling mango, and in early summer you will see heaps of green Rajapuri in Gujarati markets sold specifically for athanu.
Many vendors simply call these 'athana ni keri' — pickle mangoes — and households that make their own achar often have a trusted seller they return to every season.

sections.h2: What makes a good pickle mango
list: Firm flesh that holds its shape after salting, drying and weeks in oil.
Strong sourness so the finished pickle tastes sharp and lively rather than flat.
Low fibre so pieces bite cleanly instead of turning stringy.
Thick flesh for a good yield of pieces from every fruit.
Pale, cream-white flesh when cut, a sign the fruit has not started to ripen.

sections.h2: Why Rajapuri suits Gujarati pickle styles
p: Gujarati pickles ask a lot of the mango. Katka Keri needs small, even cubes that stay crunchy. Chhundo needs flesh that grates into firm shreds and holds up while sugar dissolves around it. Gor Keri and Meethi Keri need chunks that stay whole in a thick sweet syrup. Methia keri needs fruit sour enough to stand up to fenugreek.

That is why Rajapuri mango for pickle is such a dependable choice. Its size makes cutting and grating efficient, its firmness keeps texture through the long maturing period, and its sourness balances the oil, salt, chilli and sweetness that different recipes add.

Alphonso and Kesar are prized for eating ripe — Kesar is Gujarat's own famous table mango. Raw, they are less sharply sour than pickling varieties and their flesh softens quickly, so a pickle made with them tends to go mushy and taste flat.

Raw Kesar or Alphonso can still be used for quick fresh preparations such as a raw mango chutney or a summer drink. For a pickle that is meant to last and keep its bite, cooks choose a firm, sour pickling mango instead.

Rajapuri is not the only answer. In south India, Totapuri, with its pointed tip and firm flesh, is widely used for pickles. In the north, small, very sour local desi mangoes go into Punjabi-style achar. Coastal Maharashtra and Andhra have their own preferred sour varieties for summer pickles.

This is one reason pickles taste so different from region to region. The masala gets most of the attention, but the mango underneath — its sourness, firmness and size — shapes the final jar just as much.

sections.h2: How to choose raw mangoes for pickle at the market
list: Press gently with your thumb; a pickling mango should feel rock-hard, with no give.
Look for even green skin without a yellow or red blush, which signals ripening.
Pick fruit that feels heavy for its size; it usually has thicker flesh.
Avoid bruises, soft patches, cuts or black spots on the skin.
If the seller allows, cut one open: the flesh should be pale, crisp and very sour.
Buy only what you can process within a day or two, because raw mangoes keep ripening after purchase.
Wash the mangoes and dry them completely, ideally leaving them on a cloth for a few hours.
Cut with a dry knife or a traditional sudi; remove any soft inner portion around the stone.
Cut pieces to suit the recipe and keep them as even as possible so they cure at the same pace.
Rub with salt and turmeric and rest so the pieces release their water.
Drain well and dry the pieces in the sun or a warm, airy room until dry to the touch.
Mix with masala and oil and pack into clean, completely dry jars.
Using fruit that has started to ripen — the pickle turns soft and sweet-tasting.
Leaving water on the skin or knife — moisture is the quickest route to mould.
Cutting very uneven pieces — small ones go soft while large ones stay raw inside.
Mixing batches bought days apart — they may be at different stages and behave differently.
Skipping the draining step — the released water thins the masala and shortens keeping quality.

sections.h2: How the mango shows up in a finished jar
p: When you open a good mango pickle, the pieces should hold their shape on the spoon and give a clean bite. The sourness should come through clearly under the spice rather than being masked by salt or oil.

Over weeks and months the pieces soften gradually and the flavour becomes rounder. That slow change is normal. A pickle that turns mushy very early is usually a sign that the mango was too ripe or that moisture got in.

If you are not making your own, look at the texture described on the product page and read the ingredient list. The Pickle Affair's Homemade Mango Pickle and Katka Keri are spicy raw mango pickles made from traditional Kathiawadi recipes, and Meethi Keri is the sweet option. All are made in small batches with no synthetic colours.
Whichever jar you buy, store it in a cool, dry cupboard and use a dry spoon so the mango keeps its bite for as long as possible.

faqs: Which mango is best for pickle?
Firm, sour raw mangoes with thick flesh. In Gujarat, Rajapuri mango for pickle is the traditional choice; Totapuri and local sour varieties are used in other regions.
Can I make pickle with Alphonso or Kesar?
You can, but raw Alphonso and Kesar are less sour and soften quickly, so the pickle tends to turn mushy. They are better eaten ripe.
Is Rajapuri eaten ripe as well?
Yes, it can be eaten ripe, but it is best known in Gujarat as a raw pickling mango.
What is Ladva mango?
Ladva is a local name you may hear in Gujarat pickle markets for another firm raw mango sold for achar. Names vary from market to market, so ask the seller and judge by firmness and sourness.
How do I know a raw mango is right for pickle?
It should feel rock-hard, have even green skin, feel heavy, and show pale, crisp, very sour flesh when cut.
Why does my homemade mango pickle go soft quickly?
Usually the mango had started to ripen, the pieces were not dried well, or water got into the jar. Firm fruit, thorough drying and a dry spoon help.
Does the mango variety change the taste of pickle?
Yes. Sourness, firmness and size all affect the final texture and flavour, which is one reason pickles differ so much between regions.
topics.conclusion: The mango decides the pickle. Rajapuri mango for pickle has stayed a Gujarati favourite because its firm, sour flesh keeps its crunch and carries the masala, and the same qualities are worth looking for in any jar you make or buy.

topics.title: Sun-Dried Pickle Process: Why Traditional Achar Uses the Sun
topics.excerpt: How the traditional sun-dried pickle process works, what the sun does to mango achar, how to do it hygienically, and what to look for when buying.
topics.quick_answer: In the traditional sun-dried pickle process, salted raw mango pieces are spread in strong sun so they lose moisture before they meet the masala and oil. That keeps the pickle from spoiling without vinegar and firms the texture. For sweet pickles like Chhundo, the sun also slowly dissolves the sugar into a thick syrup.

p: In Indian pickle kitchens the sun does three different jobs. First, it dries salted raw mango pieces so they lose their excess water. Second, in some homes it warms the filled jar for a few days so the masala settles into the fruit. Third, for sweet pickles such as Chhundo, it gently 'cooks' the mango and sugar into a thick syrup without a stove.
A spicy keri achar mainly needs the first, while Chhundo relies on the third. Together they make up the traditional sun-dried pickle process.

Water is what mould and yeast need to grow. Raw mango is full of it, so traditional pickle-making is really a long effort to remove water and keep it out. Salt draws water from the cut pieces; the sun then evaporates it.

Drying also concentrates the mango's sourness and makes the flesh denser, so it absorbs oil and spice rather than diluting them. A pickle that starts with properly dried pieces holds its flavour and texture far better than one made from wet fruit.

sections.h2: The sun-dried pickle process, step by step
list: Choose firm, sour raw mangoes; wash them and dry the skins completely.
Cut into pieces suited to the recipe, using a dry knife and board.
Rub the pieces with salt and turmeric and leave them to rest, covered, so they release water.
Drain off the liquid; many cooks squeeze it out gently or let the pieces drip in a basket.
Spread the pieces in a single layer on a clean cotton cloth in direct sun, covered with thin muslin.
Turn them during the day and bring them indoors before evening so they do not pick up dew.
Repeat over the following days until the pieces are dry to the touch, then mix with masala and oil.

p: There is no fixed number of hours. It depends on the strength of the sun, the humidity, the size of the pieces and how much water the mango released. In strong summer sun, small pieces dry faster than large chunks; on a hazy day the same batch can take noticeably longer.

Experienced cooks judge by feel. The pieces should be dry on the surface, slightly shrunken at the edges and free of any beads of liquid, but not hard or leathery. Over-dried pieces can turn tough and chewy in the jar.

sections.h2: Sun-cooking sweet pickles like Chhundo and Gor Keri
p: Traditional Chhundo is made by mixing grated raw mango with sugar and a little salt and turmeric, then keeping the covered jar in the sun day after day. The sugar draws out juice, the warmth dissolves it, and the mixture slowly thickens into a glossy syrup. The jar is stirred with a dry spoon daily and brought in each evening; chilli and cumin are usually added once the syrup is ready.

Gor Keri follows a similar idea with jaggery, which melts into a dark, thick coating around mango chunks. Many homes today use a gentle stove method for speed, but the sun method is the older, slower way.

sections.h2: What the sun does to texture and flavour
list: Firmer pieces that stay crisp in oil rather than turning soggy.
Concentrated sourness, because the same flavour sits in less water.
Better spice absorption, since denser flesh soaks up masala and oil.
Brighter colour, with turmeric settling evenly into the surface of the mango.
A thicker, glossier syrup in sweet pickles made by the sun method.
Use a freshly washed, fully dry cotton cloth or a clean steel tray.
Dry on a raised surface such as a table or a clean terrace, not on bare ground.
Cover with thin muslin or a fine net to keep out dust, insects and birds.
Handle pieces with clean, dry hands or a dry spoon.
Bring everything indoors before evening and on any day that looks like rain.
Keep the drying area away from smoke, traffic and cooking fumes.
Skipping the draining step — the released water ends up in the jar and thins the masala.
Leaving pieces out overnight — dew undoes the day's drying.
Piling pieces in thick layers — the bottom pieces stay damp and dry unevenly.
Over-drying — pieces turn leathery and never soften properly in oil.
Packing into a damp jar — a few drops of water can undo all the sun's work.

p: India has many valid pickle styles. Some regional pickles are cooked, some are made with vinegar, and some are quick fresh pickles meant to be eaten within days. Each has its own taste and purpose.

Traditional Gujarati and Kathiawadi mango pickles rely mostly on salt, oil, spices and dryness, which is why the sun matters so much in them. Sun-drying is slow, depends on the weather and needs space, so some commercial pickles use vinegar or added preservatives instead. That changes the taste — vinegar adds its own sharp acidity — and often the texture too.

sections.h2: What to look for when buying
p: Start with the ingredient list. If you want a traditional-style achar, check whether vinegar or added preservatives are listed, and read how the maker describes their method on the product page. A clear label, a named maker and an FSSAI licence number are basic signs of a responsible producer.

The Pickle Affair, a brand of Arham Foods packed in Maharashtra under FSSAI licence 21521053000490, makes Homemade Mango Pickle, Katka Keri and Chhundo from traditional Kathiawadi recipes in small batches, with no synthetic colours. Check each product page for ingredients.

sections.h2: After the sun: storing the finished jar
p: Once a sun-dried pickle is bottled, the goal is to keep it as dry as the day it was made. Store the jar in a cool, dark cupboard, close the lid firmly after every use and always use a clean, completely dry spoon.
Keep the pieces covered by oil, and press them down if they rise above it. Follow the label for best-before guidance, and discard the pickle if you see mould, fizzing or notice an off smell.

faqs: Why are pickles dried in the sun?
To remove moisture from salted mango pieces so the pickle keeps well without vinegar, stays firm and absorbs the masala properly.
How long are pickles sun-dried?
Usually a few days, depending on the strength of the sun, humidity and the size of the pieces. Cooks judge by feel: dry to the touch but not leathery.
Is sun-drying hygienic?
Yes, when done on a clean cloth or tray on a raised surface, covered with muslin, and brought indoors before evening. These are long-standing household practices.
Can I dry mango pieces indoors instead?
Yes. On cloudy or rainy days, many cooks spread the pieces on a cloth in a warm, airy room under a fan. It takes longer, but it is better than packing damp pieces.
Does sun-dried pickle need vinegar?
Traditional Gujarati mango pickles generally do not. They rely on salt, oil, spices and dryness instead.
Why is Chhundo kept in the sun?
In the traditional method, the sun slowly dissolves the sugar and thickens it into a syrup around the grated mango, without cooking on a stove.
topics.conclusion: The sun-dried pickle process is slow and weather-dependent, but it is what gives traditional achar its firm bite and keeping quality. Whether you dry mango at home or buy a jar, look for dryness, clear labels and a maker who respects the old method.

topics.title: Barni: The Traditional Clay and Ceramic Pickle Jar Explained
topics.excerpt: What a barni is, why Indian homes stored achar in ceramic jars, how to choose and care for one, and whether glass does the same job today.
topics.quick_answer: A barni is the traditional glazed ceramic or clay jar Indian homes use to mature and store pickle. Its thick, opaque walls keep the pickle cool and dark, and a good glaze does not react with salt, oil or sourness. A clean glass jar kept in a dark cupboard does much the same job today.

p: A barni is a squat, wide-mouthed jar, usually glazed ceramic in cream, brown or a two-tone finish, with a fitted lid. In older homes, rows of barnis stood in a cool storeroom, each holding a different pickle — keri achar in one, Gunda Keri in another, Chhundo in a third.
The barni pickle jar goes by other names too: martaban in Hindi and Urdu, and bharani in parts of south India.

Most pickle barnis are glazed ceramic or stoneware. The glaze matters most: unglazed clay is porous, so it absorbs oil and moisture, can hold old smells and is harder to keep clean. A smooth, fully glazed interior stays non-reactive and wipes clean.

Lids are usually ceramic. Traditionally, a piece of clean cotton or muslin was also tied over the mouth, under or over the lid, to keep out dust and insects while letting the jar breathe during the early maturing days.

list: Thick walls kept the temperature inside steady through hot afternoons and cool nights.
Opaque sides blocked light, which can dull the colour and flavour of pickle over time.
A non-reactive glaze did not interact with salt, oil or the sourness of mango.
A wide mouth made it easy to stir, press pieces under the oil and serve with a long, dry spoon.
A heavy base kept the jar stable on storeroom shelves and floors.

sections.h2: How a barni was used through the year
p: In pickle season, the freshly mixed achar went into a large, dry barni, often with muslin tied over the top. Some families set the barni in the sun for a few days so the masala settled, then moved it to a cool, dark corner to mature.

The big barni was rarely opened daily. Instead, a small jar for the kitchen was filled from it with a dry ladle every week or two. That habit kept the main stock away from steam, wet spoons and frequent opening — one of the smartest pickle-keeping practices our grandmothers followed.

list: Glazed barni — non-reactive, blocks light, keeps temperature steady; heavy and can crack if dropped.
Glass jar — non-reactive and easy to clean; lets light in, so keep it in a dark cupboard.
Stainless steel — fine for serving and short-term storage; many families still prefer ceramic or glass for long maturing.
Plastic — not ideal for long storage; oil, salt and sourness can interact with some plastics and leave lingering smells.
Aluminium, iron or copper — avoid, as salt and acid can react with these metals.

sections.h2: How to choose a barni pickle jar today
list: Check that the inside is fully glazed, smooth and even, with no rough or bare patches.
Look for cracks, chips or fine crazing in the glaze; these can trap oil and moisture.
Buy from a seller who confirms the glaze is food-safe.
Make sure the lid sits snugly and does not rock.
Choose a size you will finish comfortably; a huge barni that is opened rarely suits a family stock, a smaller one suits daily use.
Lift it; a good barni feels solid and well balanced.

sections.h2: Preparing a barni before you fill it
list: Wash the barni and lid with hot water and a mild dishwashing liquid.
Rinse thoroughly so no soap smell remains.
Dry it upside down, then leave it open in the sun or a warm, airy spot until completely dry inside.
Smell the inside; it should smell of nothing at all.
Fill it only when you are sure there is no trace of moisture on the walls, base or lid.

sections.h2: Transferring pickle from a store jar
p: If you have a family barni, you can move pickle into it at home. Use a clean, completely dry spoon or ladle, transfer the pieces first and pour the oil over the top so the masala stays covered. Wipe the rim before closing the lid.

Keep the original jar's label or take a photo of it, so you still have the best-before and storage details. Do not mix an old batch with a new one in the same barni; finish one, clean and dry the jar, then refill it.

Between batches, soak the barni in warm soapy water to loosen old oil, then scrub gently with a soft brush. Rinse well and dry completely before storing it with the lid off, so no stale smell builds up inside.
Avoid sudden temperature changes, such as boiling water poured into a cold barni, which can crack ceramic.

list: Filling a barni that is not fully dry — the most common cause of mould.
Using a wet or used spoon — it carries water and food particles into the jar.
Keeping the barni near the stove — heat and steam reach the pickle every time it is opened.
Ignoring hairline cracks — they hold old oil and can harbour moisture.
Leaving pieces above the oil — exposed masala dries out or spoils first.

sections.h2: Do you need a barni to enjoy good pickle?
p: No. A barni is lovely to own and part of many family memories, but what it really offers is darkness, steady temperature and a non-reactive surface. A clean glass jar in a dark, cool cupboard gives you those same conditions, as long as you use a dry spoon and keep the lid firmly closed.

Pickles such as The Pickle Affair's Gunda Keri, Katka Keri and Chana Keri Methi Achar, made from traditional Kathiawadi recipes in small batches, can stay in the jar they arrive in. Follow the label, and move them to a barni only if you enjoy the ritual.

faqs: What is a barni?
A traditional glazed ceramic or clay jar with a wide mouth and lid, used in Indian homes to mature and store pickle.
Is a barni better than a glass jar for pickle?
Both are non-reactive. A barni blocks light and keeps temperature steadier; a glass jar works just as well when kept in a dark, cool cupboard.
Can I store pickle in plastic?
It is better to use glass or glazed ceramic. Oil, salt and sourness can interact with some plastics over time and leave lingering smells.
What is the difference between a barni and a martaban?
They are largely the same thing. Martaban is a common Hindi and Urdu name for a glazed ceramic storage jar, while barni is widely used in Gujarati and Hindi homes.
Should I use an unglazed clay pot for pickle?
It is not ideal for long storage. Unglazed clay is porous, so it absorbs oil and moisture and is harder to keep clean.
How do I remove an old pickle smell from a barni?
Soak it in warm soapy water, scrub gently, rinse thoroughly and leave it open to dry fully in the sun or a warm, airy place before refilling.
Do I need to transfer bought pickle into a barni?
No. Keep it in its own jar in a cool, dark cupboard and follow the label. Transfer it only if you prefer, using a completely dry jar and spoon.
topics.conclusion: A barni pickle jar kept achar cool, dark and clean long before modern packaging. You can still enjoy one today, but a glass jar in a dark cupboard, a dry spoon and a firmly closed lid will keep your pickle just as well.

topics.title: Mango Pickle 1 kg: Why Two 500 g Jars Beat One Big Jar
topics.excerpt: Want mango pickle 1 kg at a time? Why two 500 g jars stay fresher than one big jar, and how to plan quantity and styles.
topics.quick_answer: If you want mango pickle 1 kg at a time, buy two 500 g jars rather than one large jar. One jar stays sealed while the other is in use, so the last spoonful tastes as good as the first. You can also split the quantity across two or three mango styles for more variety on the table.

sections.h2: Why one big jar goes stale faster
p: Every time a jar is opened, air, kitchen humidity, and the chance of a stray drop of water get in. A large jar that takes many weeks to finish is opened again and again, and the pickle at the bottom has had the most exposure by the time you reach it.

The oil level drops as you spoon out pieces, and the last portion can taste flat compared with the first. Splitting the same quantity into two jars halves the exposure, because the second jar stays sealed until you need it.

sections.h2: Two 500 g jars vs one 1 kg jar
list: Freshness — with two jars, half your pickle is untouched until the first jar is finished.
Oil cover — a smaller jar keeps the pieces under oil for longer, because the level drops less before you open the next one.
Risk — if a wet spoon or a loose lid spoils one jar, the other half is still safe.
Handling — a 500 g jar is easier to lift, pour from, and store on a normal kitchen shelf.
Flexibility — two jars can be two different styles, or one can be given to a relative or neighbour.

sections.h2: How much mango pickle your household really uses
p: Before ordering mango pickle 1 kg at a time, think about how often a spoon actually goes into the jar. Quantity should follow habit, not the idea that more is always better value.
list: Family of four eating pickle at most meals — 1 kg as two 500 g jars is a sensible stock.
Couple eating pickle a few times a week — one 500 g jar, or a 500 g jar plus a 250 g jar of a second style.
Single person or occasional use — a 250 g jar at a time; reorder when it is nearly finished.
Joint family or a house with daily guests — 1 kg or more, always split into several sealed jars.
Tiffin packers — count the dabbas you pack each week; a spoonful per tiffin adds up faster than you expect.

p: If you were planning 1 kg of one pickle, consider 500 g of your everyday style plus 250 g each of two others. For example, a jar of the classic Homemade Mango Pickle for daily meals, a smaller jar of Katka Keri for chunky bite, and a jar of Meethi Keri for the sweet side of the plate. You get the same quantity with far more variety.

This is close to how many Gujarati kitchens have always worked: a large stock of the everyday keri achar, alongside smaller amounts of sweet and specialty pickles brought out for particular meals. The combo pack collection groups jars that sit well together if you prefer not to choose one by one.

sections.h2: Which mango style suits which meal
list: Classic Homemade Mango Pickle — dal-bhaat, khichdi, curd rice, and plain rotli; the everyday all-rounder.
Katka Keri — chunky pieces with bite, good with rich parathas, kadhi-khichdi, and bajra rotla.
Meethi Keri — sweet and tangy, good with thepla, puri, and for family members who prefer less heat.
Mixed thali — one spicy and one sweet mango pickle side by side covers most tastes at the table.

sections.h2: Storing the second jar until you need it
list: Check that the lid is tight and the seal is intact when the parcel arrives.
Keep the sealed jar in a cool, dark cupboard away from the stove, sink, and sunny windows.
Store it upright so the oil stays evenly over the pickle.
Do not open it 'just to taste'; every opening lets in air and moisture.
Open it only when the first jar is nearly finished, using a clean, dry spoon.
Follow the best-before date and storage note printed on the label.

p: The open jar is where most problems begin. Always use a dry steel spoon, never one that has touched dal, curd, or water. Close the lid straight after serving, and wipe any masala from the rim so the lid seals properly.
Press the pieces down now and then so they stay under the oil. Many families fill a small serving jar once a week and keep the main jar closed in the cupboard.

sections.h2: When a bigger quantity makes sense
p: There are times when 1 kg or more is the right order: a family function, festive hosting, a large joint family, or stocking up for someone moving to a new city. The principle stays the same. Buy the quantity, but in several sealed jars, and open them one at a time.

sections.h2: What to check when buying mango pickle in larger quantity
list: The label — ingredients, net weight, packing date, best-before date, and storage note.
FSSAI details — the licence or registration number and the name of the business that packs it. The Pickle Affair is a brand of Arham Foods, packed in Maharashtra under FSSAI licence 21521053000490.
Style — whether it is a spicy oil-based pickle, a sweet pickle, or a chunky cut, so you do not end up with a large stock of a style nobody enjoys.
Colour — a natural turmeric-and-chilli colour is a good sign; our pickles use no synthetic colours.

sections.h2: Common mistakes with a 1 kg order
list: Buying a full kilo of a style nobody has tasted yet.
Opening both jars at once so that each can be 'tried'.
Keeping the jar next to the stove, where heat and steam reach the lid.
Topping up an old jar with pickle from a new one, mixing older pickle with fresh.
Ignoring the label because 'pickle lasts forever'; always follow the best-before date.

faqs: Do you sell mango pickle in a 1 kg jar?
Our jars are 250 g and 500 g; check the product page for the sizes currently listed. For 1 kg, two 500 g jars keep the pickle fresher than one large jar.
How long does 500 g of mango pickle last a family?
It depends on habit. A family that eats pickle at most meals will finish it much faster than one that uses it occasionally. Watch how quickly your first jar empties and plan from there.
Is buying 1 kg better value than 250 g?
Larger jars usually cost less per gram, so compare on the product page. The real value comes from finishing the pickle while it is at its best, which is easier with two 500 g jars.
Can I split 1 kg across different mango pickles?
Yes. A common split is 500 g of your everyday mango pickle plus 250 g each of a chunky and a sweet style.
Should I refrigerate the second jar?
Usually not. A sealed jar keeps well in a cool, dark cupboard; follow the storage note on the label.
Which mango pickle should I buy in the larger quantity?
The one your family already eats every day. Keep specialty or sweet styles in smaller jars until you know how fast they go.
topics.conclusion: For mango pickle 1 kg at a time, order two 500 g jars and open them one after the other. Or split the quantity across an everyday, a chunky, and a sweet mango pickle for the same amount with more variety.

topics.title: 250 g vs 500 g Pickle Jar: Which Size Should You Order?
topics.excerpt: 250g vs 500g pickle: a simple way to choose a jar size by household, eating habits, pickle style, and how new the style is to you.
topics.quick_answer: Order 250 g when the style is new to you or pickle is an occasional side; order 500 g for a style your family already eats every day. The larger jar often works out cheaper per gram, but a jar finished while it is fresh is always the better buy.

sections.h2: The short rule: try in 250 g, stock up in 500 g
p: The 250g vs 500g pickle question comes down to one thing: how quickly you will finish the jar. Pickle tastes best when it is eaten within a reasonable time of opening, with the pieces still under oil and the masala bright. A jar that sits half-used for months is not good value, whatever its size.
So the simplest rule is to try a new style in 250 g and move to 500 g once you know your family loves it. That way, you never end up with a large jar of something nobody reaches for.

list: Have you tasted this style before? If not, choose 250 g.
Does someone in the house eat pickle at most meals? If yes, choose 500 g of that everyday style.
Will the jar be finished comfortably before its best-before date, with room to spare? If you are unsure, choose 250 g.
Single person or student — 250 g; small jars suit occasional use and small kitchens.
Couple — 250 g of each style you like, or 500 g of a favourite you eat daily.
Family of four — 500 g of the everyday pickle, plus 250 g jars of anything new.
Joint family or frequent guests — 500 g jars, opened one at a time.
Elderly parents living alone — 250 g jars are lighter to handle and get finished while fresh.

p: Different pickles are eaten at different speeds, which matters as much as household size.
list: Everyday spicy mango pickles such as Katka Keri or the classic keri achar go with dal-bhaat and rotli daily, so 500 g usually makes sense once you know you like them.
Sweet relish pickles such as Chhundo get used quickly in homes where children eat thepla or khakhra often; elsewhere, 250 g is enough.
Specialty pickles such as Gunda Keri or Chana Keri Methi have a distinct texture and flavour. Start with 250 g even if you plan to become a regular buyer.
Jaggery pickles such as Gor Keri are rich, and most families use a little at a time; 250 g is a good starting point.

sections.h2: Value per gram vs value per spoonful
p: Larger jars often cost less per gram, so compare the two sizes on the product page. But the number that really matters is how many spoonfuls you enjoy. If a 500 g jar loses its best flavour before you finish it, the saving disappears.

A practical way to think about it is the cost of pickle you actually eat. For a style you finish quickly, 500 g is excellent value. For a style you use once a week, two 250 g jars bought a few months apart may serve you better than one large jar opened for a long time.

Each opening lets in air and humidity. A 500 g jar is opened roughly twice as many times as a 250 g jar before it is finished, and as the level drops, more of the pickle sits above the oil. The masala on exposed pieces can dry out or darken.

Smaller jars are finished sooner and the oil cover stays good for longer. That is why many families who eat a lot of pickle still prefer two smaller jars to one big one: the second stays sealed until it is needed.

sections.h2: Two 250 g jars or one 500 g jar?
p: If you want 500 g in total, two 250 g jars give you choice. They can be two different styles, such as Chhundo and Chana Keri Methi, so the family can compare a sweet and a savoury pickle side by side. Or they can be the same style, with one jar staying sealed.
One 500 g jar is simpler for a style you already eat every day. There is less to store and fewer lids to manage, and if the jar is finished quickly, freshness is not a concern.

Gift sets work best as several 250 g jars in different styles. The receiver can discover a favourite without being stuck with a large jar of something they do not enjoy, and a set of small jars looks generous on a festive tray.
For a family you know well, a 500 g jar of their favourite is a more practical gift. If you are not sure of their taste, pair one sweet and one spicy 250 g jar; that covers most households.

sections.h2: Sizes for tiffin, travel, and small kitchens
p: Hostel rooms, PG accommodation, and small apartment kitchens often have little cupboard space and warmer temperatures. A 250 g jar fits easily, is finished sooner, and is less of a loss if something goes wrong.

For tiffin, do not carry the main jar at all. Spoon a little into a small steel or glass dabba with a tight lid each day. For long journeys or sending pickle to someone studying away from home, a 250 g jar is lighter and easier to pack safely.

sections.h2: Signs you picked the wrong size
list: The jar ran out within days — move that style up to 500 g next time.
The jar has been open for months — drop to 250 g, or buy it less often.
Pieces at the bottom are dry or above the oil — the jar is too large for how often you use it.
One style always empties first — that is your family's everyday pickle; buy it in the larger size.
A jar keeps getting pushed to the back of the shelf — keep that style for occasional 250 g orders.

faqs: What sizes do The Pickle Affair jars come in?
Our jars are 250 g and 500 g. Check each product page for the sizes currently available.
Which size is better value, 250 g or 500 g?
The 500 g jar often costs less per gram, so compare on the product page. Choose the size you will finish while the pickle is at its best.
Which size should I choose for a pickle I have never tried?
250 g. It is the low-risk way to find out whether your family enjoys a new style.
Which size should I gift?
Several 250 g jars in different styles usually make a better gift than one large jar, unless you know the family's favourite.
Is 500 g too much for a couple?
Not if you eat that pickle most days. For occasional use or a new style, 250 g is easier to finish.
Does a bigger jar need the fridge?
Jar size does not change the storage advice. Keep it in a cool, dark cupboard with a tight lid and follow the label.
Should I buy two 250 g jars instead of one 500 g jar?
If you want variety or use pickle slowly, yes. For a daily favourite, one 500 g jar is simpler.
topics.conclusion: In the 250g vs 500g pickle decision, let habit choose: try new styles in 250 g and stock your everyday favourite in 500 g. That rule keeps every jar fresh and avoids waste.

topics.title: Pickle Without Preservatives: How Traditional Achar Keeps
topics.excerpt: How can pickle last months without added preservatives? Salt, oil, spices, sun-drying, and what to check on the label.
topics.quick_answer: Traditional pickle keeps because of salt, oil, sun-drying, and spices — the same methods used for centuries — rather than added chemical preservatives like sodium benzoate. Check the ingredient list: it should read like a kitchen recipe.

list: Salt draws water out of the fruit and makes it inhospitable to spoilage.
Sun-drying removes more moisture.
Oil seals the surface from air.
Spices like mustard, fenugreek, turmeric, and chilli add flavour and help preservation.
Sugar or jaggery in sweet pickles also acts as a preservative.

sections.h2: What 'no preservatives' should mean on a label
p: Look for the absence of sodium benzoate, potassium sorbate, acetic acid or vinegar used as a preservative, and synthetic colours. Salt, oil, sugar, and spices are ingredients, not added preservatives in this sense.
If a label says 'no preservatives' but lists vinegar or acidity regulators, read carefully.

sections.h2: Your part in keeping it fresh
p: Pickles without chemical preservatives depend more on storage: a dry spoon, a sealed lid, and a cool, dark cupboard. Moisture is the main risk.
Follow the best-before guidance on the jar and discard any jar that shows mould or an off smell.

sections.h2: Why many commercial pickles add preservatives
p: A pickle sold across the country has to survive warehouses, long transit in heat, months on a shop shelf, and irregular handling in a home kitchen. Manufacturers who want a long, predictable shelf life under all of those conditions often add preservatives as insurance.

Another reason is recipe changes. Pickles made with less salt or less oil — to reduce cost or to appeal to buyers watching salt — lose part of their natural protection. Something has to replace it, and that is usually vinegar, an acidity regulator, or a chemical preservative.
Traditional recipes avoid this by keeping salt and oil at levels that preserve the pickle on their own.

sections.h2: Common additives and what they do
list: Sodium benzoate — limits the growth of yeasts and moulds in acidic foods.
Acetic acid or vinegar — raises acidity quickly so the pickle is stable without long maturation.
Citric acid and other acidity regulators — adjust sourness and pH, usually shown with INS numbers.
Sulphites such as potassium metabisulphite — used in some preserved foods to prevent spoilage and browning.
Synthetic colours — not preservatives, but often added to keep batches visually identical.

p: Salt and oil are what let a traditional pickle skip preservatives. Salt pulls water out of the mango and makes the environment hostile to spoilage; oil keeps air away from the surface. Reduce either one sharply and the pickle becomes more fragile.

That is why a genuinely low-salt, low-oil pickle usually needs either refrigeration or added preservatives. If you see one without either, read the label closely. With traditional achar, the answer is portion size: a teaspoon of a properly salted pickle goes a long way.

This is also why traditional pickle tastes so strong. The high salt and spice levels that keep it stable are exactly why a small amount flavours a whole meal, so a jar lasts longer than you might expect.

sections.h2: Signs a preservative-free jar is going off
list: Fuzzy white, green, grey, or black growth anywhere in the jar.
A sour-alcoholic or musty smell instead of a spicy one.
Fizzing or bubbles rising when the jar is opened.
A slimy texture on the mango pieces.
Any of these means discard the jar — do not scoop out the affected part and keep the rest.

p: Look for a clear ingredient list, the name of the manufacturer or packer, an FSSAI licence number, and a best-before date. These tell you someone is accountable for the jar. The Pickle Affair is packed by Arham Foods under FSSAI licence 21521053000490.

Also consider how the jar will reach you. A well-sealed glass jar packed to prevent leaks protects the pickle on its journey; once it arrives, move it to a cool, dark cupboard and open it with a dry spoon.

When the parcel arrives, check that the seal is intact and the jar has not leaked before you store it. Note the best-before date on the label, and if you have more than one jar, open the one with the earliest date first.

Salt, oil, and spices protect pickle very well, but they cannot undo contamination. A wet spoon, a lid left open in the monsoon, or a jar stored beside a steaming pot can introduce enough moisture for mould to grow, even in a well-made pickle.

That is not a weakness of traditional pickle so much as a reminder that it was designed for careful handling. The families who kept pickle for a whole year in barnis also followed strict habits: dry hands, dry spoons, and jars opened only when needed.

list: The ingredient list reads like a recipe: mango, oil, salt, spices, and sugar or jaggery if sweet.
No sodium benzoate, vinegar used as a preservative, or synthetic colour.
A named manufacturer or packer with an FSSAI licence number.
A best-before date and storage instructions.
At home: dry spoon, pieces under oil, lid closed, cool cupboard.

sections.h2: How long a traditional pickle stays good
p: There is no single answer for every jar, because shelf life depends on the recipe, the salt and oil levels, and above all how the jar is handled once opened. That is why the best-before date printed on the jar is the figure to follow, rather than a general rule of thumb.

Within that window, flavour keeps evolving. Many people find a traditional mango pickle tastes best a few weeks after it is made, once the masala has fully soaked into the mango and the raw edge of the spices has softened.

An opened jar that is handled well — dry spoon, lid closed, pieces under oil — usually stays in good condition for a long time. One that is handled carelessly can spoil within days, preservatives or not. Handling matters as much as the recipe.

faqs: Can pickle last without preservatives?
Yes. Salt, oil, sun-drying, and spices have preserved pickle for centuries.
Is salt a preservative?
Salt preserves, but it is a basic ingredient; 'no preservatives' usually means no added chemical preservatives.
How do I store preservative-free pickle?
Cool, dark cupboard; sealed lid; clean dry spoon every time.
What preservatives are common in store-bought pickle?
Sodium benzoate, vinegar or acetic acid, acidity regulators, and sometimes sulphites. Check the ingredient list for them.
Why do low-salt pickles need preservatives?
Salt is one of the main natural preservatives in pickle; reducing it removes part of that protection.
Does sugar count as a preservative in pickle?
Sugar and jaggery help preserve sweet pickles naturally, but they are treated as ingredients rather than added chemical preservatives.
Should preservative-free pickle be kept in the fridge?
Traditional oil-cured pickles usually keep in a cool cupboard. Follow the storage note on the jar and use a dry spoon.
topics.conclusion: Traditional pickle does not need chemical preservatives — it needs good ingredients and good storage habits.

topics.title: Pickle Gift for Diwali: How to Build a Thoughtful Achar Hamper
topics.excerpt: Planning a pickle gift for Diwali? How to build an achar hamper that suits different tastes, with tips on sizes, presentation, and timing.
topics.quick_answer: For a pickle gift for Diwali, combine one sweet and one or two spicy jars in 250 g sizes, for example Chhundo, Katka Keri, and Gunda Keri. Pickle is used every day, lasts well beyond the festival, and stands out for families who already receive plenty of sweets. Add a short note on pairings and storage.

sections.h2: Why pickle works as a Diwali gift
p: Diwali brings boxes of mithai and dry fruit, and many homes receive more than they can finish before the sweets go stale. Pickle is different. It is used at everyday meals for weeks after the festival, and each spoonful is a small reminder of the person who sent it.

A set of regional pickles also feels personal. Traditional Gujarati and Kathiawadi pickles carry the taste of home kitchens, which is exactly what many people miss during the festive season, especially those living far from family.

There is a seasonal logic too. In many Gujarati homes, the year's keri achar is made in summer when raw mangoes arrive, and by Diwali those jars have had months to mature. Sharing pickle at this time of year continues an old habit of sending a jar of the house achar to relatives and neighbours.

list: Families who receive many sweet boxes — a savoury gift is welcome after a week of mithai.
Gujarati families living away from home — familiar keri achar and Chhundo bring back the taste of their own kitchens.
Elders — many grandparents enjoy a good pickle with simple meals and appreciate traditional styles.
Colleagues and clients — a neat set of small jars is practical and easy to share at home.
Friends who love to cook — specialty pickles such as Gunda Keri are a new ingredient to explore.

p: The best pickle gift for Diwali covers more than one taste, so everyone in the household finds something they enjoy.
list: Sweet — Chhundo or Meethi Keri for children, elders, and anyone who prefers less heat.

Specialty — Gunda Keri or Chana Keri Methi for something less common and very Gujarati.
Jaggery — Gor Keri for families who love the deep sweetness of gor in their food.

sections.h2: Matching the hamper to the household
list: Young family with children — two sweet jars and one mild-to-medium spicy jar.
Spice-loving household — Katka Keri, Gunda Keri, and Chana Keri Methi, with one sweet jar for balance.
Elderly couple — two small jars of familiar styles rather than a large assortment.
Someone new to Gujarati food — Chhundo and the classic mango pickle, which are the easiest introductions.
Office gifting — the same simple sweet-plus-spicy pair for everyone keeps things fair and easy.

p: Small 250 g jars are ideal for gifting. The receiver can try each style without being left with a large jar of something they do not like, and three small jars look more generous than one big one.

For close family whose favourite you already know, a 500 g jar of that pickle is a practical, much-used gift. You can also mix sizes: a 500 g jar of their everyday pickle with a 250 g jar of something new.

Pickle jars look festive with very little effort. Arrange them in a cane basket or on a steel thali, tie a cotton or bandhani cloth around each lid, and add a diya or a few marigolds for Diwali colour. A plain kraft box with dried leaves or paper shreds works well for colleagues.
Keep the jars upright and snug so they do not knock together, and leave the original labels visible. The label carries the ingredients, best-before date, and storage note, which the family will need.

sections.h2: Write pairing notes for each jar
p: A short handwritten card turns a set of jars into a thoughtful gift, because it tells the family exactly how to use each one.
list: Chhundo — with thepla, khakhra, or spread on a paratha for a tiffin.
Katka Keri — with dal-bhaat, kadhi-khichdi, or a rich stuffed paratha.
Gunda Keri — with bajra rotla, khichdi, or curd rice.
Meethi Keri — with puri, thepla, or as the sweet side of a festive thali.

sections.h2: Pairing pickle with other Diwali treats
p: A pickle hamper sits naturally alongside Gujarati Diwali snacks. Add a pack of khakhra, some mathiya or chorafali, or a box of thepla for travel, and the hamper becomes a ready snack plate for the days after the festival.
If you are giving mithai as well, a single jar of Chhundo or a spicy mango pickle beside the sweet box adds contrast without making the gift too large.

Order well before Diwali. Courier networks get busy during the festive season, and you will want time to check each jar and assemble the hamper. Check the estimated delivery shown at checkout rather than assuming a date.
If you are sending jars straight to a relative in another city, enter their address at checkout and let them know a parcel is on its way, so someone is at home to receive it.

list: Unpack the parcel as soon as it arrives.
Check that each jar is intact with no cracks.
Make sure every lid is tight and the seal is unbroken.
Wipe any oil from the rim or outside of the jar with a dry cloth.
Keep the jars in a cool, dark cupboard until you wrap them.

p: Add one line on storage to your card: keep the jars in a cool, dark cupboard, use a clean, dry spoon every time, and follow the label. Most families know this already, but a reminder protects your gift.
If the household is very small, suggest they open one jar at a time and keep the others sealed. That way each pickle is enjoyed at its best long after Diwali.

faqs: Is pickle a good Diwali gift?
Yes. It is practical, used at everyday meals, and stands out among boxes of sweets and dry fruit.
Which pickles should I include in a Diwali hamper?
One sweet pickle such as Chhundo plus one or two spicy styles such as Katka Keri or Gunda Keri covers most tastes.

topics.title: FSSAI Licence for Pickles: What It Means and How to Verify It
topics.excerpt: What an FSSAI number on a pickle jar tells you, how to look it up on the official FoSCoS portal, and what it does not guarantee.
topics.quick_answer: An FSSAI licence or registration number on a pickle jar shows that the business behind it is registered with India's food safety regulator. You can look the number up on FSSAI's official FoSCoS portal and check that the business name matches the label. The Pickle Affair is packed by Arham Foods under FSSAI licence 21521053000490.

p: FSSAI is the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, the national regulator for food safety. Food businesses that make, pack, store, or sell food come under its framework, and the number you see on a food label links that product to a business on the regulator's records.

For pickle buyers, this matters because achar is often bought from small brands, home-style kitchens, and online stores. A visible FSSAI licence for pickles gives you a way to find out who is actually responsible for the jar in your hands.

sections.h2: What the number on a pickle jar tells you
p: The FSSAI number printed on a label, usually next to the FSSAI logo, identifies the food business behind the product. It tells you that the business is on record with the regulator and can be traced, which is useful if you ever have a question or complaint about a product.
It also helps you tell the difference between a brand name and the business that stands behind it. The name on the front of the jar is the brand; the FSSAI number points to the registered business.

sections.h2: What the number does not tell you
list: It is not a taste or quality rating. Two licensed brands can make very different pickles.
It does not describe the recipe. Check the ingredient list for oil, sweetener, spices, and any additives.
It does not tell you freshness. Look for the packing date and best-before date on the label.
It is not a health claim. Pickle is a condiment; enjoy it in small portions as part of a balanced meal.
It does not replace your own checks. A good seal, clean jar, and natural colour still matter.

sections.h2: Registration and licence: the general difference
p: You will see both words used. In general terms, FSSAI issues a basic registration to smaller food businesses and a licence to larger ones, and both come with a number that can be printed on the label. For a buyer, either one means the business is on the regulator's records.

The categories, thresholds, and procedures are set by FSSAI and can change, so this guide does not quote them. If you are a seller wondering which one applies to you, the official FSSAI website and FoSCoS portal are the right places to check.

sections.h2: Where to find the FSSAI number
list: On the jar label — usually beside the FSSAI logo, often near the manufacturer, packer, or marketer details.
On the brand's website — many brands show it in the footer, on product pages, or on an About page.
On the outer packaging — gift boxes and cartons may repeat it.
By asking — a genuine seller should be happy to share the number and the registered business name.

sections.h2: How to verify an FSSAI number on FoSCoS
p: FoSCoS (Food Safety Compliance System) is FSSAI's official online portal. Menu names can change over time, but the steps below describe the general process.
list: Note the full FSSAI number exactly as printed on the jar or website.
Open the official FoSCoS portal through the FSSAI website, rather than a third-party site.
Look for the public option to search or verify a food business by licence or registration number.
Enter the number and view the details shown for that business.
Compare the business name and address with the manufacturer or packer named on the label.
Check that the record appears to be current rather than expired or cancelled.
Name matches — the business name should match the packer, manufacturer, or brand owner printed on the jar.
Location makes sense — the address or state should be consistent with where the label says the pickle was packed.
Record is current — if it looks expired or no result appears, ask the seller before buying.
No result at all — re-check the digits first; a single typing error is the most common reason.

sections.h2: One business, several brands, more than one number
p: A single food business can sell under more than one brand name, so different brands may show the same number. The Pickle Affair is a brand of Arham Foods, which is why you will see Arham Foods named alongside our licence number.
Some labels also show more than one number, for example when one business makes or packs the food and another markets it. What matters is that each number leads back to a business named on the label.

sections.h2: Why this matters for handmade pickles bought online
p: Many people now buy traditional achar online from small makers rather than from a local shop where they know the family. When you cannot see the kitchen, the FSSAI number, a clear label, and an identifiable business are how you know who made your pickle.
Small-batch and handmade do not have to mean informal. A brand can follow a traditional Kathiawadi recipe, make it in small batches, and still be fully on record with the regulator.

list: Ingredients — listed so you know the oil, sweetener, and spices used.
Net weight — useful when comparing jar sizes.
Packing and best-before dates — the best guide to freshness.
Storage instructions — follow these over general advice.
Vegetarian symbol — the green mark on vegetarian food.
Contact details — a way to reach the business if you have a question.

p: The Pickle Affair is a brand of Arham Foods. Our pickles follow traditional Kathiawadi recipes, are made in small batches without synthetic colours, and are packed in Maharashtra under FSSAI licence 21521053000490.

You are welcome to look the number up on FoSCoS yourself. Then judge our Homemade Mango Pickle, Gor Keri, or Gunda Keri the way any pickle should be judged: by the label, the ingredients, and the taste.

faqs: What does FSSAI on a pickle jar mean?
It means the food business behind the jar is registered or licensed with India's food safety regulator and can be identified by its number.
How do I check an FSSAI number?
Search the number on FSSAI's official FoSCoS portal and match the business name and address with the label.
Does an FSSAI licence mean a pickle is good quality?
No. It shows the business is on record with the regulator. Judge quality by ingredients, freshness, and taste.
Why do two brands show the same FSSAI number?
One registered business can sell under more than one brand name.
Do small or home-based pickle sellers need FSSAI registration?
FSSAI's framework covers food businesses of different sizes, including smaller ones. For the exact requirement in a particular case, check the official FSSAI website or FoSCoS.
What if an FSSAI number shows no result?
Re-check the digits, then ask the seller for the registered business name. Be cautious if they cannot explain it.
What is The Pickle Affair's FSSAI licence number?
Our pickles are packed by Arham Foods in Maharashtra under FSSAI licence 21521053000490.
topics.conclusion: An FSSAI licence for pickles tells you who stands behind the jar, not how good the pickle is. Look the number up on FoSCoS, match the business name, and then judge by the label, the ingredients, and the taste.

topics.title: How Pickles Are Shipped in Glass Jars (and What to Check on Arrival)
topics.excerpt: How pickles are shipped in glass jars, what changes in transit, and exactly what to check when your pickle parcel arrives.
topics.quick_answer: Pickles are usually shipped in sealed glass jars because glass does not react with oil, salt, or sour mango. A well-packed jar travels upright, cushioned, and with a tight lid. When the parcel arrives, check the box for oil stains, the jar for cracks, and the lid for a firm seal before you open it.

p: Pickle is oily, salty, and acidic, and it sits in its container for a long time. Glass is non-reactive, so it does not take on flavours or interact with the oil and sour mango. It is also easy to clean, and it lets you see the pickle before you open it.

In older homes the same job was done by glazed ceramic barnis. Glass does it today because it is easier to seal and travels more reliably. The trade-off is weight and fragility, which is why packing matters so much.

sections.h2: What keeps a jar from leaking
p: Leaks usually start at the rim. A jar that is filled cleanly, with no oil or masala left on the rim, gives the lid a proper seal. A little headspace at the top lets the contents move slightly without pressing against the lid.

Oil-based pickles are designed to have a layer of oil over the pieces. In transit that oil moves around, so a tight lid matters more than anything else. Sweet pickles like Chhundo have a thick syrup that moves less, but still need a well-sealed lid.

sections.h2: How a well-packed pickle parcel is put together
list: Sealed lid — tightened firmly, often with an inner seal under the cap.
Wrap around the jar — so glass does not touch glass or the sides of the box.
Cushioning — filler around and between jars so they cannot shift.
Upright position — jars standing up so oil stays over the pickle and away from the lid.
Sturdy outer box — strong enough to handle stacking during transit.
Handling marks — fragile or this-side-up labels help, though good packing should not depend on them.

sections.h2: What happens to pickle during transit
p: Parcels are lifted, stacked, and sometimes tilted. Inside the jar, the oil moves up and down, masala settles at the bottom, and pieces may shift away from the surface. Long journeys in warm weather can also make the oil thinner and the jar warm to the touch.

None of this harms the pickle. Once the jar rests upright in a cool place, the oil settles back over the pieces and the masala sits where it should. That is why the first step after delivery is simply to let the jar rest.

sections.h2: Oil-based vs sweet pickles in transit
list: Oil-based pickles such as Katka Keri — oil may separate or coat the inner rim; it settles once the jar rests.
Sweet pickles such as Chhundo — thick syrup moves less, but may look a little uneven after a long journey.
Jaggery pickles such as Gor Keri — syrup may thicken in cool weather or loosen in heat; both are normal.
Chunky pickles — pieces may sit higher than usual; press them down gently with a dry spoon.
Look at the outer box before opening: is it dry and free of oil stains?
Unpack carefully and check each jar for cracks or chips, especially at the neck.
Check that the lid is tight and any seal is unbroken.
Hold the jar upright and look for oil seeping around the lid.
Check the label for the product name, net weight, and best-before date.
Move the jar to a cool, dark cupboard and let it rest before opening.

sections.h2: What is normal and what is not
list: Normal — a little oil on the outer rim or under the lid from movement; wipe it with a dry cloth.
Normal — oil separated at the top or masala settled at the bottom; it evens out at rest.
Normal — cloudy oil or thick syrup in cool weather; it clears at room temperature.
Not normal — a cracked or chipped jar, even if it is not leaking.
Not normal — a broken seal, a loose lid, or the box soaked with oil.
Not normal — an unusual smell or visible mould when you first open the jar.

p: If a jar arrives cracked, chipped, or leaking, do not eat from it; small glass fragments may not be visible. Keep the jar and packing as they are and take clear photos of the jar, the lid, the label, and the box.
Then contact us through the Contact page with your order details and the photos, so we can look into it quickly. Please do not throw the jar away before you have taken photos.
Let the jar stand upright for a while before opening, so the oil and masala settle. Wipe the outside and the rim with a dry cloth, then open it with a clean, dry spoon.

If you have ordered several jars, open one at a time and keep the rest sealed in a cool, dark cupboard away from the stove and sunlight. Follow the storage note on the label; most oil-cured and sweet pickles do not need the fridge.

Once a jar is finished, wash it in hot soapy water and dry it completely in the sun or on a rack. Clean glass jars are useful for storing spices, dry snacks, or a small serving portion of pickle for the dining table.
Cushioning and boxes can be kept for sending pickle or other jars to family. Make sure any reused box is clean, dry, and strong enough for glass.

Many people send a jar of achar to a son or daughter in another city. Use the original sealed jar if possible, wrap it well, stand it upright in a snug box with filler on all sides, and seal the lid with tape for extra security.
Place the jar in a zip bag before wrapping it, so a small leak does not spoil the rest of the parcel. Mark the box as fragile and tell the receiver to check the jar the same way you would.

faqs: Why are pickles shipped in glass jars?
Glass does not react with oil, salt, or acid, keeps flavours clean, and lets you see the pickle.
Is oil on the lid normal after delivery?
A little oil on the rim is normal after transit. Wipe it with a dry cloth and check that the lid is still tight.
What if my jar arrives broken or cracked?
Do not eat from it. Take photos of the jar and packing and contact us through the Contact page with your order details.
Why has the oil separated in my pickle?
Movement during transit separates oil and masala. Let the jar rest upright and it settles again.
Should I refrigerate pickle after delivery?
Usually not. Most oil-cured and sweet pickles keep in a cool, dark cupboard; follow the label.
Can I open the jar immediately?
You can, but letting it rest upright for a while first lets the oil settle back over the pieces.
Can I reuse the glass jar?
Yes. Wash it in hot soapy water, dry it completely, and use it for spices or a small serving jar.
topics.conclusion: Knowing how pickles are shipped makes the arrival check simple: dry box, intact jar, tight lid. Let the jar rest upright, wipe the rim, and store it in a cool, dark cupboard before opening with a dry spoon.
