p: Gujarati cooking balances sweet, sour, salty and spicy on one plate, and its pickles followed. Alongside spicy mango and Gunda Keri, Gujarati kitchens built a family of sweet pickles with jaggery and sugar, such as Gor Keri and Chhundo.

Kathiawad and Saurashtra kept a hotter, more rustic style, with stuffed gunda, chilli pickles and coarse masalas suited to millet rotla. The Pickle Affair follows these traditional Kathiawadi recipes in small batches.

sections.h2: What history teaches about choosing pickle today
p: The principles that kept pickles safe for generations still matter: good raw produce, enough salt, clean and dry equipment, a proper layer of oil or syrup, and patience while the pickle matures.

When you buy a jar, look for signs of that care: a clear ingredient list, a licence number, storage advice and a best-before date. At home, a dry spoon and a closed lid continue the job your grandmother's barni once did.

faqs: How old are Indian pickles?
Pickling in India is very old and has been practised for many generations, but there is no single reliable date for when it began.
Where does the word achar come from?
It is often said to have Persian roots, while regional words like athanu, lonche and oorugai have long been used in local languages.
Did Indian pickles always contain chilli?
No. Chilli reached India through trade several centuries ago; before that, heat came from pepper, mustard and ginger.
Why do Indian pickles use so much oil?
Oil forms a protective layer that keeps air away from the pieces, which helps the pickle keep and lets the masala mature.
Why are pickles traditionally made in summer?
Raw mangoes are in season and the strong sun helps dry the pieces and warm the jars as the pickle matures.
Which is the oldest Indian pickle?
There is no reliable answer. Pickling developed in many regions at once, using whatever produce each area had.
topics.conclusion: The history of Indian pickles is a story of seasons, salt and family kitchens, with each region adding its own flavour. Every jar you open today, sweet or spicy, carries a little of that long tradition.

topics.title: Grandmother's Pickle Tips: Baa's Rules for Achar That Lasts
topics.excerpt: Grandmother's pickle tips from a Gujarati kitchen: Baa's rules on dryness, mangoes, masala, jars, oil, serving and spotting trouble.
topics.quick_answer: The most important grandmother's pickle tips are simple: keep everything bone dry, choose firm sour mangoes, salt and drain the pieces, use fresh spices, keep the pickle under oil or syrup, and always serve with a dry spoon from a small jar. These habits, passed down by Baa, prevent mould and keep the flavour bright.

p: Every Gujarati family seems to have a grandmother whose pickle was the benchmark. Her secret was rarely a rare spice. It was a set of habits she followed every single time, many of which sound fussy until you see a batch spoil without them.
These grandmother's pickle tips come from that tradition. They apply whether you are making a summer batch of keri athanu at home or simply looking after a jar you have bought.

Ask any Baa and the first rule is dryness. Water is the main reason homemade pickle grows mould, so mangoes are washed well ahead of time and dried completely, knives and chopping boards are wiped dry, and hands are dried before touching anything.
Jars are washed and left in the sun until there is no trace of moisture. Even the ladle used for mixing is kept only for pickle, so it never picks up water from other cooking.

Baa never made pickle on a cloudy, humid or rainy day. She waited for a run of dry, sunny weather so the cut pieces and jars could dry properly. Mangoes were often washed the evening before and left to dry overnight, so cutting could start early.

She also cleared the whole day. Pickle-making is not something to rush between other chores, and a batch started in a hurry is the one most likely to be put away damp. Many families still write the date on a slip of paper tied to each jar.

list: Pick firm, raw mangoes with tight, unblemished skin.
Press gently: there should be no soft patches or bruises.
Taste a sliver; a good pickling mango is clearly sour.
Cut pieces of even size so they cure at the same pace.
Discard any piece with dark spots near the stone.

p: Before any masala goes in, Baa rubs the cut mango with salt and turmeric and leaves it to rest. The salt draws out water, which collects at the bottom of the vessel.

The pieces are then drained and spread on a clean cloth to dry, usually in shade or gentle sun, until the surface feels dry to the touch. Skipping this step leaves too much water in the fruit and is one of the most common reasons homemade pickle spoils.
Old spices make dull pickle. Baa buys rai kuria (split mustard) and methi kuria (split fenugreek) fresh for the season and smells them before use; they should be sharply aromatic.
Red chilli powder should be bright, not brown, and hing strong enough to notice from across the kitchen. Masala is mixed on a dry plate and added to the mango only when everything is completely dry.

sections.h2: The right jar and the muslin cloth
p: Traditional pickle is stored in a ceramic barni or a thick glass jar. Both are non-reactive, which matters with sour mango and salt. Baa avoids reactive metal containers for long storage.

For the first days, many grandmothers tie a clean muslin cloth over the mouth of the jar instead of closing the lid, then sun the jar during the day. The cloth keeps dust and insects out while letting moisture escape. Once the pickle settles, the lid goes on.

In the first days, the pickle is stirred with a dry ladle so the masala and oil reach every piece. Baa does not rush it: a new pickle tastes harsh and salty, and it needs time for the flavours to settle.
Sweet pickles follow their own rhythm. Chhundo, for example, is traditionally set in the sun or cooked gently until the sugar becomes a thick syrup. Patience here is part of the recipe.

For spicy pickles, the most repeated instruction is to keep the pieces covered. Oil acts as a seal against air and moisture. If the level drops below the pieces, many families top it up with oil that has been heated and cooled completely.
Sweet pickles like Gor Keri rely on their jaggery syrup instead. Pressing the pieces down with a dry spoon so they stay coated does the same job.

list: Fill a small serving jar for daily use and keep the big jar closed.
Use a dry spoon every time; never a spoon that has touched other food.
Never return leftover pickle from a plate to the jar.
Close the lid straight after serving.
Keep jars in a cool, dark cupboard away from the stove and window.

p: Some changes are normal. Pickle darkens, softens and develops a deeper flavour as it matures. Oil may separate, and sweet pickles may thicken or form sugar crystals in cold weather.
Other signs mean the batch should go. Fuzzy mould, an off, sour-milk or alcoholic smell, fizzing or bubbling, or a slimy texture are warnings. Baa's rule was simple: when in doubt, throw it out.

sections.h2: Applying the tips to a bought jar
p: Not every grandmother's tip applies to a sealed, labelled jar. There is no need to sun it or tie muslin over it; follow the storage instructions and best-before date printed on the label instead.

The serving habits, though, matter just as much. A jar of The Pickle Affair's Homemade Mango Pickle or Katka Keri stays in good condition for longer when you use a dry spoon, keep the pieces under oil and close the lid tightly.

faqs: What is the most important pickle tip from grandmothers?
Keep everything completely dry. Water on the mango, jar, spoon or hands is the most common cause of mould.
Why do grandmothers tie a cloth over the pickle jar?
A muslin cloth keeps dust and insects out while letting moisture escape in the first days of sunning.
Why is mango salted before adding masala?
Salt draws out water, which is drained away so the pickle is less likely to spoil.
What should I do if the oil level drops?
Many families top it up with oil that has been heated and cooled completely, so the pieces stay covered.
Can I put pickle back in the jar after serving?
No. Leftover pickle from the plate can carry moisture and food particles that spoil the whole jar.
Do I need to sun a bought pickle jar?
No. Store it as the label advises and use a dry spoon; sunning is for homemade batches.
Is it normal for homemade pickle to taste very salty at first?
Yes. A new pickle often tastes harsh and salty; the flavour mellows as the masala and mango settle together over time.
topics.conclusion: Grandmother's pickle tips come down to dryness, patience and clean habits. Follow them at home or with a bought jar, and your pickle will taste the way Baa intended.

topics.title: Famous Pickles of India: A Region-by-Region Guide
topics.excerpt: Famous pickles of India by region: from Andhra avakaya and Rajasthani ker sangri to Bengali kasundi, Northeast bamboo shoot and Gujarati Chhundo.
topics.quick_answer: India's famous pickles change with every region: fiery mango avakaya and gongura from Andhra, mustard-oil achar from Punjab, ker sangri from Rajasthan, lonche from Maharashtra, tender mango and lime pickles from the South, kasundi and mustard-oil pickles from Bengal, bamboo shoot pickle from the Northeast, and sweet Chhundo and Gor Keri from Gujarat.

p: India's pickles follow its produce, oils and climate. Where mustard grows, mustard oil fills the jar; where mangoes are abundant, mango dominates; where the air is dry, sun-cured pickles keep well. Spice preferences, local fruit and family habits do the rest.

The examples below are some of the best-known pickles of each region. Every state has many more, and recipes vary from district to district and family to family, so treat this as a starting map rather than a complete list.

sections.h2: Gujarat: sweet and spicy side by side
p: Gujarat is known for keeping sweet and spicy pickles together on one shelf. Chhundo, grated raw mango with sugar and spice, and Gor Keri, mango in a jaggery masala, are the famous sweet styles.

On the spicy side are Katka Keri, Chana Keri Methi with chickpeas and fenugreek, and Gunda Keri, which pairs mango with sticky gunda berries. Kathiawadi kitchens in particular make these hot and robust.

sections.h2: Rajasthan: desert produce and bold chilli
p: Rajasthan's dry climate shaped pickles from hardy desert produce. Ker sangri, made from the small ker berry and sangri beans, is one of the state's most distinctive foods and is also pickled.

Stuffed red chilli pickle, with large chillies filled with spiced masala, is a well-known Rajasthani favourite, and lasode ka achar, made with gunda berries, is loved in Rajasthan as much as in Gujarat.

Punjabi aam ka achar is pungent and bold, made with mustard oil and spices such as fennel, nigella and fenugreek. Mixed vegetable achar is common too, and in winter many homes make a sweet-sour pickle of cauliflower, carrot and turnip.
Across Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, stuffed red chilli pickle, jackfruit pickle and lemon pickle are household names, usually made with mustard oil and cured in the sun.

sections.h2: Maharashtra, Goa and the Konkan coast
p: In Marathi, pickle is lonche. Kairiche lonche, raw mango pickle with split mustard, fenugreek and hing, is the everyday jar, and lemon and green chilli lonche are just as common.
Methamba, a sweet-sour raw mango preparation with jaggery and fenugreek, is a seasonal favourite. It is usually made in small quantities and eaten fresh rather than kept for months.

Further south, Goan pickles show a strong Portuguese influence in their use of vinegar; prawn balchão, spicy, tangy and made to keep, is the best-known example. Konkani and Malvani homes along the coast make mango and other pickles that sit somewhere between Goan and Maharashtrian styles, using whatever local produce the season brings.

Avakaya, the fiery mango pickle made with mustard powder, red chilli and oil, is perhaps the most famous pickle of the Telugu states. Mango pieces are cut with the hard shell of the stone still attached.
Gongura pickle, made from sour sorrel leaves, is another signature. Both are known for their heat and are classically eaten mixed into hot rice with ghee.

The South is famous for tender mango pickles, made from small whole baby mangoes in brine and chilli. Each state has its own name and method for them. Lime pickle is a staple across the region, eaten with curd rice.
Kerala is also known for inji puli, a sweet-sour ginger and tamarind relish served at sadya feasts, and coastal homes make fish and prawn pickles.
Bengali pickles lean on mustard oil and mustard seed. Kasundi, a sharp mustard relish, is a well-known Bengali condiment, and mango pickled in mustard oil is a summer favourite.
Sweet-sour pickles are common too, including those made from kul (Indian jujube) in winter. Many are set out in the sun on rooftops, just as in Gujarat.

The Northeast has its own pickle traditions, built on local ingredients. Bamboo shoot pickle is widely made, and pickles using very hot local chillies, such as the bhut jolokia or king chilli, are famous for their fierce heat.
Many of these pickles use fermentation and local herbs in ways quite different from western Indian methods, which makes them well worth exploring.

sections.h2: Beyond mango: the other pickles of India
p: Mango may be the most famous, but Indian kitchens pickle far more. Lemon and lime pickles are made in almost every region, in salty, spicy and sweet versions. Amla (Indian gooseberry), green and red chilli, garlic, ginger and carrot are common across the North and West.

Regional produce adds more: karonda berries in western India, jackfruit in the North and East, gongura leaves in the Telugu states, bamboo shoot in the Northeast and fish or prawn on the coasts. Gujarat adds gunda, which few other regions pickle.

list: A base of salt to draw out moisture and preserve.
A protective medium: oil, vinegar, brine, sugar or jaggery.
Seasonal produce picked at its best.
Spices chosen to suit local food and climate.
Family recipes passed down by hand and memory.

p: If you want to explore, start with one pickle from a region whose food you already like, and taste it with that region's meal. Avakaya is best with rice and ghee, Gunda Keri with bajra rotla, Chhundo with thepla.

Buy small jars, read the label for ingredients and storage advice, and use a dry spoon for every serving. A shelf of a few regional pickles is one of the easiest ways to travel India from your kitchen.

faqs: What is the most famous pickle in India?
Mango pickle is the most widely made, with famous regional versions such as Andhra avakaya, Punjabi aam ka achar and Gujarati Katka Keri.
Which Indian state is famous for pickles?
Almost every state has famous pickles. Andhra Pradesh is known for fiery ones, while Gujarat is known for sweet pickles like Chhundo.
What is a Gujarati pickle famous for?
Gujarat is known for keeping sweet pickles like Chhundo and Gor Keri alongside spicy ones like Katka Keri and Gunda Keri.
Which regional pickles are sweet?
Gujarati Chhundo and Gor Keri, Maharashtrian methamba and Kerala's inji puli are well-known sweet or sweet-sour examples.
Are all Indian pickles made with oil?
No. Many use oil, but others rely on brine, vinegar, sugar or jaggery depending on the region.
Is kasundi a pickle?
Kasundi is a sharp Bengali mustard relish. It is often grouped with pickles, though it is closer to a mustard sauce.
Which regional pickle should I try first?
Try one from a cuisine you already enjoy and eat it with that region's meal, such as Chhundo with thepla.
topics.conclusion: India's famous pickles are as varied as its kitchens, from fiery avakaya to sweet Chhundo. Try them one region at a time, with the meals they were made for.

topics.title: Gujarati vs Rajasthani Pickle: Spices, Sweetness and Shared Gunda
topics.excerpt: Gujarati vs Rajasthani pickle compared: spices, oil, sweetness, desert ingredients like ker sangri, the gunda pickle both love, and how to choose.
topics.quick_answer: Rajasthani pickle tends to be pungent and fiery, often made with mustard oil, whole spices like fennel and nigella, and desert produce such as ker and sangri or stuffed red chillies. Gujarati pickle builds on split mustard, fenugreek and hing, cuts mango small, and includes sweet styles like Gor Keri and Chhundo. Both states love gunda (lasoda) pickle.

p: Gujarat and Rajasthan share a long border, and food crosses it easily. North Gujarat, Kutch and Rajasthan's Marwar region share a dry climate, a love of millet breads and a summer pickle-making habit built around raw mango, chilli and gunda.
Yet a Gujarati pickle and a Rajasthani pickle rarely taste the same. The differences come down to oil, spices, sweetness and the desert ingredients Rajasthan is known for.

list: Typical oil — Rajasthani: mustard oil is common. Gujarati: varies by home and maker; check the label.
Key spices — Rajasthani: fennel, nigella, fenugreek, mustard, hing. Gujarati: rai kuria, methi kuria, hing, turmeric, chilli.
Heat — Rajasthani: often very hot. Gujarati: ranges from mild sweet to fiery Kathiawadi.
Sweetness — Rajasthani: mostly savoury, with sweet-sour fresh preparations. Gujarati: a full family of sweet pickles.
Signature pickles — Rajasthani: ker sangri, stuffed red chilli, lasode ka achar. Gujarati: Chhundo, Gor Keri, Katka Keri, Gunda Keri.

sections.h2: The flavour of a Rajasthani achar
p: A Rajasthani mango or chilli pickle is usually bold and pungent. Mustard oil gives a sharp bite, fennel adds a sweet aniseed note, nigella brings a slightly smoky flavour and fenugreek adds bitterness. Red chilli is used generously.

Stuffed red chilli pickle is a classic: large, fleshy red chillies are slit, filled with a spiced masala and left to mature in oil. It is fiery, tangy and meant to be eaten in small bites with roti or dal.

sections.h2: The flavour of a Gujarati achar
p: A Gujarati spicy pickle such as Katka Keri centres on methiyo masalo: split mustard seed, split fenugreek, salt, turmeric, hing and chilli. The split seeds make a grainy masala that clings to small pieces of mango.

Fennel and nigella are less common, and hing is more prominent. The result is tangy and spicy with a clean mustard sharpness. Kathiawadi versions can be just as hot as Rajasthani ones, which surprises people who expect all Gujarati food to be sweet.

Rajasthan's most distinctive pickles use produce that grows in its arid landscape. Ker is a small, sour wild berry, and sangri is the long bean of the khejri tree. Both are traditionally dried, which helps them keep through the year.

Ker sangri is best known as a dry sabzi, but it is also made into pickle, often alongside ker on its own. These ingredients are rarely used in Gujarati pickles outside the border areas, so they are a good way to taste the difference between the two states.

sections.h2: Gunda: the pickle both states love
p: Gunda, called lasoda in Rajasthan, is the fruit of the Cordia tree, common across both states. Its sticky flesh turns soft and chewy in pickle, and both Gujarati and Rajasthani families make it every summer.

In Gujarat, gunda is often paired with raw mango as Gunda Keri, stuffed with methiyo masalo. Rajasthani lasode ka achar is often more pungent, with fennel or mustard oil. Methods vary by family in both states, but the love for gunda is shared.

sections.h2: Sweetness: where the styles part ways
p: The clearest difference is sweetness. Gujarat keeps sweet pickles as everyday jars: Gor Keri with jaggery, Chhundo with sugar, and Meethi Keri.

Rajasthan enjoys sweet-sour mango too, most famously aam ki launji, raw mango cooked with jaggery, fennel and spices. But launji is usually made fresh and eaten within days, while Gujarati sweet pickles are made to keep.

list: Rajasthani mango pickle often uses larger pieces with visible whole spices.
Stuffed chillies give a soft, fleshy bite with a masala centre.
Gujarati Katka Keri uses small, even pieces for several bites per spoon.
Chhundo is grated and jammy.
Gunda in both states is soft, sticky and chewy.

sections.h2: The meals each is made for
p: Rajasthani pickles suit hearty desert food: dal baati churma, bajra roti with garlic chutney, gatte ki sabzi and kadhi. A small bite of fiery pickle cuts through ghee-rich dishes.
Gujarati pickles are built for a varied thali: thepla, rotli-shaak, dal-bhaat and khichdi, with Kathiawadi bajra rotla where Gunda Keri shines. Sweet pickles also go with farsan and travel snacks.

sections.h2: Crossing the border at the table
p: The two styles swap plates easily. Gunda Keri sits naturally beside dal baati or bajra roti, and a spoon of Gor Keri gives a sweet-sour contrast to fiery Rajasthani dishes like spicy gatte ki sabzi or ker sangri.

Going the other way, a small bite of Rajasthani stuffed red chilli pickle lifts a simple Gujarati khichdi-kadhi or plain dal-bhaat. There is no rule that a pickle must match the cuisine; it only needs to balance what is on the plate.

list: Love mustard oil, fennel and serious heat? Try a Rajasthani-style pickle.
Prefer tangy spice with hing and small crunchy pieces? Choose Katka Keri.
Want sweet-sour? Gor Keri or Chhundo.
Curious about the shared tradition? Start with Gunda Keri.
Eat bajra rotla or roti often? Both styles suit it well.

p: The same care keeps both styles in good condition: a dry spoon every time, pieces kept under oil or syrup, a tightly closed lid and a cool, dark cupboard away from the stove.
Stuffed chilli and gunda pickles soften over time, which is normal. Mould, an off smell or fizzing are not. For a bought jar, follow the label's storage advice and best-before date.

faqs: What is the difference between Gujarati and Rajasthani pickle?

Rajasthani pickle is usually pungent with mustard oil, fennel and nigella and uses desert produce like ker and sangri. Gujarati pickle uses split mustard, fenugreek and hing and includes many sweet styles.
Is lasode ka achar the same as Gunda Keri?
Both are made with gunda (lasoda) berries. Gunda Keri adds raw mango, while lasode ka achar recipes vary and are often more pungent.
Which is spicier, Gujarati or Rajasthani pickle?
Rajasthani pickles are often very hot, but Kathiawadi Gujarati pickles can be just as spicy.
What is ker sangri pickle?
A Rajasthani pickle made from ker berries and sangri beans, desert produce that is usually dried before use.
Are Rajasthani pickles sweet?
Mostly no. Rajasthan's best-known sweet-sour mango dish, aam ki launji, is usually made fresh rather than kept as a pickle.
Do Gujarati pickles use mustard oil like Rajasthani ones?
Oil varies by home and maker in Gujarat. For any bought jar, check the ingredient list on the label.
Which should I try first?
If you like sweet-sour flavours, start with Gujarati Gor Keri; if you want to taste the shared tradition, try Gunda Keri.
topics.conclusion: Gujarati vs Rajasthani pickle is a contrast between neighbours: Rajasthan's pungent, fiery desert jars and Gujarat's tangy and sweet ones. The love of gunda connects them, and both deserve a place on your shelf.

topics.title: Gujarati vs Maharashtrian Pickle: Athanu and Lonche Compared
topics.excerpt: Gujarati vs Maharashtrian pickle: athanu and lonche compared on spices, tempering, sweetness, methamba vs methia keri, and the meals each suits.
topics.quick_answer: Gujarati and Maharashtrian pickles are close cousins: both use split mustard, fenugreek, hing, turmeric and chilli with raw mango. Maharashtrian lonche often uses a cooled oil tempering and favours fresh preparations like methamba, while Gujarati athanu has a larger family of sweet keeping pickles such as Chhundo and Gor Keri, plus spicy styles like Chana Keri Methi.

p: In Marathi, pickle is lonche; in Gujarati it is athanu. The two states share a border, a long history of trade and many families who live with a foot in each culture, so it is no surprise their pickles are closely related.
Both rely on the same core spices and on raw mango in summer. The differences are in technique, sweetness and the fresh preparations each state loves.

list: Core spices — Maharashtrian: split mustard (mohari dal), fenugreek, hing, turmeric, chilli. Gujarati: rai kuria, methi kuria, hing, turmeric, chilli.
Technique — Maharashtrian: many recipes pour a cooled oil tempering over the masala. Gujarati: dry masala mixed with the mango, then covered with oil.
Sweetness — Maharashtrian: sweet-sour styles, many made fresh. Gujarati: sweet pickles made to keep.
Mango cut — Both often use small pieces; Gujarati Chhundo is grated.
Best with — Maharashtrian: varan bhaat, poli-bhaaji, bhakri. Gujarati: thepla, dal-bhaat, khichdi, rotla.

p: Maharashtrian raw mango pickle, kairiche lonche, typically starts with mango pieces salted and mixed with a lonche masala of split mustard, fenugreek, hing, turmeric and red chilli.

Many family recipes then prepare a phodni, oil heated with mustard seed, hing and turmeric, cool it completely and pour it over the pickle. This gives a slightly roasted, rounded aroma and helps the oil settle over the pieces.

sections.h2: What goes into a Gujarati keri athanu
p: A Gujarati spicy pickle like Katka Keri uses methiyo masalo, split mustard and fenugreek with salt, turmeric, hing and chilli, mixed into dried mango pieces and then covered with oil.
The masala is grainy and clings to the fruit, and hing tends to be prominent. Kathiawadi versions are hot and robust, while Chana Keri Methi adds chickpeas and extra fenugreek for depth.

Both states love mango with fenugreek, but use it differently. Maharashtrian methamba is a sweet-sour preparation of raw mango cooked briefly with jaggery and a fenugreek tempering. It is usually made in small quantities and eaten within days.

Gujarati Chana Keri Methi is a keeping pickle. Raw mango and chickpeas are coated in a fenugreek-rich masala and oil, and the flavour deepens over time. Methamba is a seasonal treat; Chana Keri Methi is a jar you keep.

sections.h2: Sweet mango: gul amba, chunda and Chhundo
p: Maharashtra has its own sweet mango traditions. Gul amba is raw mango cooked with jaggery into a soft, jam-like preserve, and chunda, grated mango with sugar and spice, is made on both sides of the border.

Gujarati Chhundo is close to chunda, and Gor Keri sets mango pieces in a jaggery masala with chilli. The difference is that Gujarati homes keep these sweet jars open every day, not only for special meals.

list: Lemon — limbache lonche in Maharashtra, limbu nu athanu in Gujarat; both have sweet and salty versions.
Green chilli — mirchiche lonche in Maharashtra; athela marcha in Gujarat.
Karonda — the small sour berry is pickled in both states.
Mango ginger — ambe halad lonche is a Maharashtrian favourite.
Gunda — a Gujarati and Rajasthani speciality, seen less in Maharashtra.

sections.h2: Thecha and sambharo: the fresh cousins
p: Both states also make fresh condiments that sit beside pickle without being pickle. Maharashtrian thecha is coarsely crushed green chilli and garlic, sharp and fiery, eaten with bhakri.
Gujarati sambharo is a lightly cooked relish of cabbage, carrot, papaya or chilli, served with farsan. Neither keeps like a pickle; they are made fresh and eaten within a day or two.

sections.h2: The meals each is made for
p: Maharashtrian lonche sits beside varan bhaat with a spoon of ghee, poli-bhaaji, pithla bhakri and thalipeeth. Its job is to add a sharp sour note to simple, comforting food. On a festive Maharashtrian thali, lonche usually takes its place on the left side of the plate with koshimbir, chutney and other small accompaniments.
Gujarati athanu goes with thepla, rotli-shaak, dal-bhaat, khichdi-kadhi and Kathiawadi bajra rotla. Sweet pickles like Chhundo also go with khakhra and farsan and on travel days.

The two styles swap plates without any trouble. A spoon of Chhundo is lovely with Maharashtrian thalipeeth or poha, and Katka Keri sits as comfortably beside varan bhaat as it does beside Gujarati dal-bhaat.

In the other direction, a tempered Maharashtrian lemon lonche suits Gujarati khichdi-kadhi, and a little thecha with bajra rotla gives a Kathiawadi meal a fresh, fiery edge. Many families living in Mumbai and Pune happily keep both on the same shelf.

list: Like a roasted, tempered aroma in your pickle? Try a Maharashtrian lonche.
Prefer a grainy, hing-forward masala? Choose a Gujarati keri athanu like Katka Keri.
Love mango with fenugreek? Chana Keri Methi keeps; methamba is a fresh treat.
Want a sweet jar for every day? Chhundo or Gor Keri.
Cooking for a mixed household? Keep one of each.

sections.h2: A Gujarati recipe, packed in Maharashtra
p: The Pickle Affair, a brand of Arham Foods, follows traditional Kathiawadi recipes and packs its pickles in small batches in Maharashtra under FSSAI licence 21521053000490. It is a small reminder of how closely the two food cultures sit together.
Whichever style you choose, the care is the same: a dry spoon, pieces kept under oil or syrup, a closed lid, a cool cupboard, and the label's storage advice for any bought jar.

faqs: What is the difference between Gujarati and Maharashtrian pickle?
Both use split mustard, fenugreek and hing, but Maharashtrian lonche often uses a cooled oil tempering, while Gujarati athanu includes more sweet keeping pickles.
What is lonche?
Lonche is the Marathi word for pickle, such as kairiche lonche (raw mango pickle) or limbache lonche (lemon pickle).
Is methamba a pickle?
Methamba is a sweet-sour raw mango preparation with jaggery and fenugreek, usually made fresh and eaten within days rather than kept.
Is chunda the same as Chhundo?
They are closely related sweet grated mango preserves made in both Maharashtra and Gujarat; recipes vary by family.
Which is spicier, Gujarati or Maharashtrian pickle?
It depends on the recipe. Both have hot styles, and Kathiawadi Gujarati pickles can be very spicy.
Do Maharashtrian and Gujarati pickles use the same oil?
Oil varies by family and maker in both states. For a bought jar, check the ingredient list on the label.
Which Gujarati pickle is closest to Maharashtrian lonche?
Katka Keri, a spicy raw mango pickle with split mustard, fenugreek and hing, is the closest everyday match.
topics.conclusion: Gujarati vs Maharashtrian pickle is a comparison of close cousins: tempered lonche and fresh methamba on one side, grainy keri athanu and sweet Chhundo on the other. Keep a jar of each and enjoy the shared spice language.
